Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Body, health & movement

breath noun

also breaths, breathing, take a breath, a deep breath, last breath, bad breath

classical

Cic. N.D. 2.136
Hor. Epod. 11.10: petītus īmō spīritus, a sigh (Lewis & Short)

spīritus, spīritūs m.

noun, fourth declension

breath, breathing; a breath

Breathing and the breath drawn: to breathe is spīritum dūcere (also “to be alive”, Cic. Fam. 10.1.1), the last breath spīritus extrēmus. Its other senses are a breeze, pride or spirit, and in Christian Latin the Holy Spirit.

Other words

  • anima, animae f. — the breath, the air breathed in and out

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 324; Ter. Ph. 868: animam compressī, I held my breath (Lewis & Short)

    Lewis & Short: anima is the air breathed, spīritus the breathing. So animam recipere, to get one’s breath back, animam continēre, to hold it (see hold one’s breath). Its other sense is the life or soul.

  • hālitus, hālitūs m. — breath breathed out, its smell; steam

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Plin. NH 21.142: ōris hālitus (Lewis & Short)

    (in poetry and post-Augustan prose)

    Bad breath is, in Pliny, animae gravitās or ōris graveolentia (M-O s.v. bad breath).

  • anhēlitus, anhēlitūs m. — panting, shortness of breath

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Plaut. As. 326–327: nōn vidēs mē ex cursūrā anhēlitum etiam dūcere?; Cic. Off. 1.131 (Lewis & Short)

    Out of breath (see pant).

Examples

  • Quid festīnās, mī Geta? Animam recipe.

    What’s the hurry, Geta? Catch your breath.Ter. Ad. 323–324

  • in pulmōnibus autem inest rāritās quaedam et adsimilis spongiīs mollitūdō ad hauriendum spīritum aptissima

    the lungs have a certain looseness, a softness like a sponge’s, made for drawing in breathCic. N.D. 2.136

  • leō cum jacēret spīritum extrēmum trahēns

    when the lion lay drawing his last breathPhaedr. 1.21.3–4

See also breathe, air, pant, hold one’s breath, let me catch my breath, lungs, phew!.
